prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of the fast-food chain Hot Indian. Hot Indian brings in $3B in annual revenues around the U.S., with locations in most major cities. Started in Minneapolis as a small food truck in 2003, Hot Indian quickly became a local staple known for their quality of food, level of service, and distinctive 'dance for 10% off' style gimmicks for customers. Hot Indian also keeps a lean menu, devised to keep operations simplified and allow for a Hot Indian location to have success in food courts, food trucks, and standalone locations alike. All restaurants are owned by the company, and each restaurant brings in about $1.5M in annual revenue at 20% operating income.
prompt.question: We have been hired to figure out where Hot Indian should source their chutney. Currently, Hot Indian sources all sauce from a company-owned manufacturing plant in Minneapolis and distributes the sauces to all locations around the country. Hot Indian has 500 additional restaurant openings planned in the next three years, and the plant will be out of capacity for the additional volume within two years. It is Day 1 of the project — how would you get the team started?

clarifying_info.q: What is the value chain of a typical store?
clarifying_info.a: Fresh produce, meats, and supplies are typically supplied through a restaurant supplier or local provider. The chutney and marinades are created in the Minneapolis facility, then shipped through a third-party distributor to restaurant locations.

clarifying_info.q: What types of items does Hot Indian have on their menu?
clarifying_info.a: Hot Indian carries two main entrees: Kati Rolls and Rice Bowls. Both come with the same 3 fillings. They have 4 sides labeled 'Snacks' and serve 'Baba's Masala Chai' in addition to traditional beverages found in fast-food operations.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a particular goal Amol Dixit has communicated?
clarifying_info.a: We're at Day 1 of the project, and Amol would like to grow operating income at the restaurants. If possible, Amol would also like to keep operations within the Minneapolis community, where he grew up and has a vested interest in. He also wants to ensure that the quality of the food at Hot Indian remains quite high in comparison to competitors while keeping operations lean.

exhibits.title: Cost Information for Different Sauce Options
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of four sauce sourcing expansion options with columns for Construction Costs, Cost per Unit, Timeline, Quality Control, and Capacity Increase. A footnote states each restaurant uses approximately 1,000 units of sauce annually.

framework: Financials: current cost of chutney production, cost to expand plant, cost of third-party suppliers, cost to do in-house at restaurant level
Operations: lead time for sauce orders, ease of ordering for restaurant managers, packaging difference impact on restaurant operations
Amol's Vision Consideration: Minneapolis community ties, quality of chutney, room to grow for the future

questions.prompt: Which sourcing option is the best for Hot Indian? Calculate the total costs for each option and compare.
questions.guidance: Candidate should first derive the number of current restaurants ($3B / $1.5M = 2,000 restaurants) and plan for 2,500 total. They should note the 2-year timeline constraint (plant out of capacity before the new build completes in 3 years) and consider a hybrid approach. Any option is defensible with sound reasoning; the suggested answer is the new Minneapolis facility supplemented by third-party supply during the build period.

math.setup: Number of current restaurants = $3B revenue / $1.5M per restaurant = 2,000. Future restaurant count = 2,000 + 500 = 2,500. Each restaurant uses 1,000 units/year. Annual sauce cost = Cost/Unit x 1,000 units x 2,500 restaurants. Total Costs = Construction Costs + Annual Sauce Cost.
steps: Create in Restaurant: Construction = $2K x 2,500 = $5M; Annual sauce = $10 x 1,000 x 2,500 = $25M; Total = $30M
Current Plant Expansion: Construction = $1.5M; Annual sauce = $4 x 1,000 x 2,500 = $10M; Total = $11.5M
Build new facility in Minneapolis: Construction = $5M; Annual sauce = $2 x 1,000 x 2,500 = $5M; Total = $10M
Third Party supplier: Construction = $0; Annual sauce = $5 x 1,000 x 2,500 = $12.5M; Total = $12.5M
Operating Income context: Current OI = $3B x 20% = $600M
math.answer: Lowest total cost is Build new facility in Minneapolis at $10M, followed by Current Plant Expansion at $11.5M, then Third Party at $12.5M, and Create in Restaurant at $30M. However, the new facility takes 3 years while the plant exceeds capacity in 2 years, so a hybrid of new facility + third-party bridge is recommended.

questions.prompt: Given the 2-year capacity constraint and 3-year build timeline for the new facility, how should Hot Indian manage the gap?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize the timing mismatch: new facility takes 3 years but capacity runs out in 2 years. A strong answer proposes using the third-party supplier (3-month lead time) as a bridge/supplement during the construction period, then transitioning fully to the new Minneapolis plant. This also satisfies Amol's preference for Minneapolis-based operations long-term.

brainstorming.prompt: The client is impressed with the sauce solution and would like the team to weigh in on an additional matter. Hot Indian is considering adding a line of lassis (an Indian yogurt beverage) to the menu. What should Hot Indian consider before adding the new item?

categories.name: Costs
ideas: Are more employees needed to prepare/serve lassis?
How much does it cost to install the equipment?

categories.name: Customer
ideas: Will it generate higher sales per order?
Is this an entrance item to get people interested in trying other Hot Indian items?

categories.name: Operations
ideas: Does it fit into current operations?
How much demand will this place on the system?
What is the rollout and implementation timeline?

recommendation: Hot Indian should build a new manufacturing plant in Minneapolis for their sauce sourcing, as it offers the lowest total cost ($10M) and the highest quality control, while honoring Amol's preference for Minneapolis community ties.
During the 3-year construction period, Hot Indian should supplement with a third-party supplier (3-month lead time) to cover the capacity gap that emerges after year 2.
risks: The promised cost per unit for the new facility may prove higher than projected — the financial case for the new build relies on the $2/unit figure holding.
If Hot Indian continues growing at the same rate beyond 500 new locations, another plant build may be needed in the future.
next_steps: Create a 5-year growth plan to determine whether additional plant builds are needed for other parts of the supply chain.
Negotiate a short-term third-party supply agreement to bridge the 1-year gap between capacity exhaustion and new plant completion.
